title: Heritage District Renovations: Updating a Character Home in Winnipeg
metaTitle: Heritage District Renovation in Winnipeg: What to Know
metaDescription: Renovating an older Winnipeg home? When a heritage permit applies, what Armstrong's Point and Crescentwood–Enderton Park mean, and what to test first.
excerpt: Most older Winnipeg houses are renovated with ordinary permits. A smaller group, on the City's List of Historical Resources or inside a heritage conservation district, needs a heritage permit too. Here is how to tell which applies to your home and how to plan around it.
answer: Most character homes in Winnipeg need only the usual building permits. Heritage rules apply when a house is on the City's List of Historical Resources or inside one of its two heritage conservation districts, Armstrong's Point and Crescentwood–Enderton Park. There, a heritage permit is needed before work that the listing or the district plan covers.

faqs.q: Do I need a heritage permit to renovate the inside of my house?
faqs.a: It depends on how the property is protected. For a property on the List of Historical Resources, a heritage permit is needed when work affects the listed character-defining elements, so check what the listing protects. For a house in a heritage conservation district, the district plan decides. Ask the City's heritage staff before you finalize the design.

faqs.q: Is every older house in Crescentwood in the heritage district?
faqs.a: No. The Crescentwood–Enderton Park heritage conservation district has a defined boundary, shown on the City's district page, so being in or near Crescentwood does not by itself put a house in it. Houses outside the boundary that are not on the List of Historical Resources follow the normal permit process, however old they are.

faqs.q: Should I test for lead paint before renovating an older home?
faqs.a: Yes, if you plan to disturb old paint. Health Canada says a home built before 1960 probably contains lead-based paint, and exterior paint on homes built from 1960 to 1990 may contain it too. Test before sanding or stripping, avoid sanders, heat guns and blowlamps, and keep children and pregnant people away from the work.

faqs.q: Can I build an addition on a house in a heritage conservation district?
faqs.a: Possibly, but treat it as a major project. The City's heritage permit page recommends a pre-application meeting, which has no fee, for additions and new infill, held at the concept or early design stage. The addition will also need the usual development and building permits that every house addition in Winnipeg requires.

faqs.q: Will a heritage permit slow down my renovation?
faqs.a: It adds a step at the start. Heritage staff review each application, and some are referred to a heritage committee or a district advisory committee, so leave time before construction begins. The City's heritage permit page does not publish a standard review time, so ask staff about current timing when you prepare your application.

blocks.x: Many older Winnipeg houses have plaster walls, tall baseboards, wood windows and front porches, and their owners usually call them character homes. That is a description, not a legal category. What matters for a renovation is whether the City protects the property, and what is behind the plaster.
Is my character home protected by heritage rules?

Only if it is on the City of Winnipeg's List of Historical Resources or inside a designated heritage conservation district. Listed resources are protected from demolition, and alterations to their protected character-defining elements need a heritage permit. A house that is simply old, and neither listed nor in a district, follows the ordinary permit process.
To check, look up the address on the City's List of Historical Resources and compare it with the district boundary maps on the City's heritage pages.

The City also keeps a Nominated List of properties being evaluated, and a Commemorative List that recognizes heritage value without restricting demolition or alterations. If anything is unclear, the City's heritage staff can be reached at [ppd-heritage@winnipeg.ca](mailto:ppd-heritage@winnipeg.ca).
What are Winnipeg's heritage conservation districts?

Winnipeg has two, both created under the City's Heritage Conservation Districts By-law. Council designated Armstrong's Point on April 25, 2019, and Crescentwood–Enderton Park on March 23, 2023. Each district has a plan that applies to every property inside its boundary, and alterations and new development there are reviewed for consistency with that plan.

blocks.x: What work needs a heritage permit?

For a listed property, any alteration that affects its listed character-defining elements. For a house in a district, whatever work the district plan requires a permit for. The City treats additions and new infill as major projects and recommends a pre-application meeting at the concept stage with the relevant heritage committee; the meeting has no fee.

Windows get specific attention. A heritage permit application for window work asks for a window condition assessment, photos of the existing windows, drawings of the originals and shop drawings of the replacements. Leave time to prepare those documents before you order anything.

A heritage permit is a separate approval. Work that needs a building, electrical or plumbing permit still needs one. We coordinate the permits and inspections a project needs with the City of Winnipeg, and heritage approval is one more step to schedule at the start. Our permit guide explains [which work needs which permit](/blog/winnipeg-renovation-permits).
What hidden issues are common in older Winnipeg homes?

Older houses can hide lead paint, materials that may contain asbestos, outdated wiring and plumbing, and framing changed by earlier renovations. None of these is a reason to avoid renovating, but each should be identified before demolition so it can be priced and handled safely instead of being discovered halfway through the job.

blocks.x: How do you modernize a character home without losing its character?

Decide early what gives the house its character, such as the trim, staircase, built-ins, windows or front porch, and plan around keeping it. Route new systems where they are least visible, match new trim and openings to the old, and keep part of the budget for repairing original materials rather than replacing them.
Keep and refinish original trim, doors and hardware where you can. They are hard to match once they are gone.
Run new wiring, plumbing and ductwork through closets, floors and the basement to avoid cutting decorative plaster.

Add insulation where walls are already open, and look at the [Efficiency Manitoba insulation rebate](/blog/insulation-rebates-during-a-renovation-manitoba) before demolition, because it must be approved first.

If windows need replacing, match the original proportions and check heritage requirements first; our guide to [window and door replacement in Winnipeg](/blog/window-and-door-replacement-winnipeg) covers permits and glass.
For more space, a [home addition](/services/home-additions) at the back of the house usually changes the street view the least.
How should you plan the budget and schedule?

Plan for discovery. In an older house, a written quote can only price what can be seen and reasonably expected, so keep a contingency for what turns up behind the plaster. If a heritage permit or hazardous-materials testing is needed, add that time before construction. Weekly progress updates help you make decisions as findings come up.

Once permits and materials are ready, most [whole home renovations](/services/whole-home-renovations) we take on run 8 to 16 weeks, and many straightforward additions take a similar time. For current price ranges by project type, see [what renovations cost in Winnipeg](/renovation-cost-winnipeg).

The City also lists heritage incentive programs. One of them, the Gail Parvin Hammerquist Fund City-wide Heritage Program, has an annual intake with a February 1 deadline for individuals and organizations. Eligibility depends on the program criteria, so ask heritage staff whether your project could qualify before you count on it.
